\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
% 2026-09-21 house shape: four setup blocks, Exp-N paragraphs (pointer -> axis -> headline -> highlight -> anomaly), case studies
% continue the numbering; no subsections; monochrome figures (ours black, STrees grey); short captions.  Numbers: tables/*.tex
% generated by make_tables.py from the records, macros in tables/*_stats.tex; case-study numbers from case/*.json.

\stitle{Hardware.}
All algorithms are implemented in C++ and run single-threaded.
%
We use a laptop (Apple M-series) and two Ubuntu 22.04 servers, server 1 and server 2 (GCC 11.4, 96 cores, 503~GB of memory each).
%
We never ran two timing runs at the same time on one machine.
%
Jobs of other users ran on the servers at the same time, with a load average of 1 to 8 on the 96 cores.
%
One core of the laptop is 1.5 to 3 times faster than one core of a server, so laptop and server latencies are not directly comparable.
%
Every table names its machine.

\stitle{Algorithms.}
\chainidx is the index of Sections~\ref{sec:index} to~\ref{sec:construction}, built by \build and queried by \query.
%
\strees is the index of Section~\ref{sec:strees}, one tree and one depth-first array per size with every value stored.
%
Its size is computed from the same core values and trees as \chainidx.
%
Its query latency is measured on the same decomposition and the same queries as \chainidx.
%
\cnd is the published counting-based nucleus decomposition~\cite{Zhang2026NucleusCounting}, which computes the core values of one clique size; it runs once per size with its default settings.
%
It computes core values only, so it is compared on build time and not on index size.

\stitle{Datasets.}
We use \numgraphs{} real graphs from five families.
%
They are collaboration graphs (\textsf{ca-*}, \textsf{com-dblp}, \textsf{dblp-*}), citation graphs (\textsf{cit-*}), web graphs (\textsf{web-*}), product co-purchase graphs (\textsf{amazon*}, \textsf{com-amazon}), and social and communication networks (\textsf{soc-*}, \textsf{com-youtube}, \textsf{email-Eu-core}, \textsf{wiki-Talk}, \textsf{loc-Brightkite}, \textsf{tech-as-skitter}).
%
They range from $1{,}005$ to $4{,}049{,}537$ vertices, with largest cliques from $7$ to $500$ vertices.
%
Table~\ref{tab:size} lists them with their largest clique size $s_{\max}$.
%
The sizes with a nonzero value are $2$ to $s_{\max}$, that is $s_{\max}-1$ sizes.
%
Three larger graphs, \textsf{com-lj}, \textsf{ca-hollywood-2009} and \textsf{com-orkut}, run out of the 503~GB of memory of the servers while the clique tree of the peel is built.

\stitle{Metrics.}
Queries draw a vertex that lies in an edge and a size $s$ between $2$ and its clique number.
%
The workload has $20{,}000$ community queries at the vertex's own level, $k=\core{s}{v}$, $20{,}000$ at half that level (rounded down, at least $1$), and $1{,}000$ at $k=1$.
%
It also has $200{,}000$ value queries.
%
Each workload runs six times.
%
The first run warms up, and the latency is the median over the other five of the total time divided by the number of queries.
%
Index sizes are measured in memory.
%
Build times exclude the reading of the graph.
%

\expsection{Index size}
Table~\ref{tab:size} lists every graph with its number of chains, its vertices per chain and its share of values stored explicitly.
%
The next three columns are the sizes of \chainidx and of \strees and their ratio, and the last two the build time and memory usage of \build (Exp-6).
%
\chainidx is \ratiomin$\times$ to \ratiomax$\times$ smaller than \strees, median \ratiomedian$\times$.
%
The ratio grows with the number of vertices per chain.
%
\emailcore, with $1{,}005$ vertices in $667$ chains, $1.5$ per chain, is the worst case at \ratiomin$\times$.
%
\webuk, with $129{,}632$ vertices in $839$ chains, $154$ per chain, and cliques of $500$ vertices, is the best at \ratiomax$\times$.
%
The two collaboration graphs with the largest cliques, \textsf{ca-coauthors-dblp} and \textsf{dblp-coauthor}, compress by $45.8\times$ and $12.0\times$.
%
The web graphs compress by $5.7\times$ to $48.7\times$, and the social graphs by $2.9\times$ to $15.9\times$.
%
If the graph keeps its original vertex ids, the index also stores the permutation from ids to labels (Section~\ref{sec:labels}), $n$ labels, which lowers the ratios to \permmin$\times$ to \permmax$\times$ (median \permmedian$\times$).

\expsection{Size by part}
On the collaboration, web and product graphs the per-size trees with their run arrays are $58$ to $74$ percent of the index.
%
The records of the chains (Section~\ref{sec:values}) are $23$ to $41$ percent.
%
On the social and citation graphs, where chains are shorter, the records reach $44$ to $58$ percent.
%
Most of a record is the trajectory, one node id per chain and size.
%
The vertex-to-chain map is $3$ to $13$ percent.
%
The values are a small part everywhere, since only the residues are stored (Theorem~\ref{thm:tail}).
%
Table~\ref{tab:size} gives, for every graph, the share of the pairs $(v,s)$ with a nonzero value whose value is a residue: it ranges from \storedmin{} percent to \storedmax{} percent, with a median of \storedmedian{} percent.
%
\webuk has $23.5$ million such pairs and stores one residue in total; \emailcore stores \storedmax{} percent of its values.
%
% 2026-09-22 moved from the former Remark 5.10 (LEDGER.md: dblp pairs 1,246,933; residues 84,010 per vertex, 9,737 per chain).
On \dblp, $84{,}010$ of $1{,}246{,}933$ pairs are residues, and stored once per chain they are $9{,}737$ values.
%
The share is lowest on the graphs with large cliques, where most of a vertex's values lie in its tail.
%
It is highest on the sparse social and citation graphs, where the certification point is close to the clique number.

\expsection{Design study}
Table~\ref{tab:layouts} measures the layout decisions one at a time on five graphs.
%
Each column is one layout, and each cell is the size of that layout on one graph.
%
Trees over twin classes (Section~\ref{sec:chains}) do not help, since twin classes have $1.03$ to $1.28$ vertices on average.
%
Trees over chains with an explicit vertex-to-chain map are $2.5\times$ to $4.5\times$ smaller than \strees.
%
Aligned labels remove the map and turn answers into ranges, and the runs with their entries give the final sizes.
%
We also measured the skyline layout of SGL~\cite{SGL} over chains, which stores one entry per chain and non-dominated size.
%
Over chains it took $1.01$ to $1.12$ times the space of the tree layout and $2.3$ to $6.3$ times longer to answer an own-level query, so it is not part of the index.

\expsection{Query latency}
Table~\ref{tab:queries} reports the own-level community query and the value query.
%
The community columns are the time to locate a community, the number of ranges of the answer, its size, and the time to list it as vertex labels.
%
The table also gives the two times of \strees, which lists a community by copying its slice of the array, on the same queries.
%
Locating takes \locmin{} to \locmax{}~ns, median \locmedian{}~ns.
%
A community of $1.9$ million vertices on \textsf{dblp-coauthor}, the graph of $4$ million vertices, is located in $11$~ns and listed in $167~\mu$s.
%
At the own level \strees locates in about half the time of \chainidx.
%
It reads the own node from the vertex directly, whereas \chainidx maps the vertex to its chain first and then reads the trajectory and the entry.
%
Listing costs \pervmin{} to \pervmax{}~ns per vertex on the graphs whose mean answer has at least a thousand vertices.
%
On \emailcore and \textsf{ca-GrQc}, whose answers have fewer than a hundred vertices, the fixed cost of a query dominates.
%
The listing time of \strees divided by that of \chainidx ranges from \stmin{} to \stmax{} (median \stmedian) over the \stpoints{} (graph, level) points of the three levels, and \chainidx is the faster one on \stfaster{} of them.
%
A run is reported as one range however many labels it expands to.
%
\chainidx is therefore faster where the answer is a few long ranges, on the social, product and web graphs, and slower where the answer is split into many short ranges.
%
\emailcore, \textsf{cit-HepPh} and \textsf{ca-AstroPh} have $2$ to $5$ vertices per range, and there one range costs as much as tens of copied labels.
%
Value queries take \valmin{} to \valmax{}~ns, median \valmedian{}~ns.
%
The slowest is \webuk.

Figure~\ref{fig:regimes} shows the three levels of the workload for both indexes on the \stpairs{} (graph, machine) pairs of Table~\ref{tab:queries} that have both indexes.
%
The left panel plots the listing time against the mean size of the answer, one point per graph and level.
%
The right panel plots the locating time by level.
%
Listing time grows linearly with the size of the answer at every level, for \chainidx and for \strees alike, at $0.05$ to $0.5$~ns per vertex above a fixed cost of a few nanoseconds.
%
On these pairs, locating costs a median of \ownmedian{}~ns at the own level, \halfmedian{}~ns at half the level and \rootmedian{}~ns at $k=1$.
%
With the jump pointers, the climb to the root at $k=1$ costs no more than the own-level query, which does not climb.
%
The half-level climb stops at an interior node and costs at most \halfmax{}~ns.
%
The parent-pointer climb of \strees has no such bound: at the half level and at $k=1$ it costs up to \stlocdeepmax$\times$ the time of \chainidx.
%
On \textsf{ca-coauthors-dblp}, whose hierarchy has $5{,}543$ levels, the half-level climb takes $1{,}086$~ns for \strees against $109$~ns for \chainidx.

\expsection{Latency by clique size and by answer size}
Figure~\ref{fig:profile} separates two variables that the workload above averages, the clique size and the answer size, on two representative graphs measured on server 2, \textsf{web-BerkStan} and \textsf{cit-Patents}.
%
The other graphs of Table~\ref{tab:queries} show the same trends.
%
Panel (a) plots the locating time against the clique size, and panel (b) the listing time against the clique size.
%
Panel (c) plots the listing time against the answer size.
%
Panels (a) and (b) use $5{,}000$ own-level queries per clique size $s$, with the vertex drawn uniformly among the vertices that lie in an $s$-clique.
%
\chainidx locates in \proflocmin{} to \proflocmax{}~ns at every size, highest between $s=3$ and $6$, where the per-size trees have the most nodes.
%
\strees locates in \profstlocmin{} to \profstlocmax{}~ns.
%
At $s=2$ and $3$, where the answers are large and consist of a few long runs, \chainidx lists the answer in \profsmallinvmax{} to \profsmallinvmin{} times the time of the memory copy.
%
From $s=4$ on, where the own-level answers shrink and spread over many ranges, the copy is faster.
%
It is up to \profbigmax$\times$ faster at $s=\profbigs$ on \textsf{cit-Patents}, where the mean answer has \profbigout{} vertices in \profbigranges{} ranges.
%
Panel (c) sorts the $20{,}000$ own-level queries of the workload above by answer size into ten groups of equal count.
%
Below $10^5$ vertices the copy is \profdeclowmin$\times$ to \profdeclowmax$\times$ faster.
%
Between $10^5$ and $10^6$ the gap closes, and from $10^6$ vertices on the two agree within \profdechigh{} percent.
% 2026-09-22 filler pass: the closer (constant per range vs per label) was said in Exp-4.

\expsection{Construction}
The last two columns of Table~\ref{tab:size} give the build time of \chainidx and its memory usage.
%
The build time covers the clique tree, the peel of every size, and the index passes: the trees, the trie of the chains, the runs and the values (Section~\ref{sec:construction}).
%
The index passes are a few percent of the total.
%
The peel and its clique tree are the rest, and the memory usage is that of the clique tree.
%
The build takes $0.01$~s on \textsf{ca-GrQc} and $221$~s on \textsf{dblp-coauthor}, the graph of $4$ million vertices, with $8.8$~GB of memory there.
%
\dblp is built in $0.84$~s with $157$~MB.

\expsection{Scalability}
Figure~\ref{fig:scale} follows \textsf{cit-Patents} and \textsf{web-BerkStan} through vertex-induced random samples of $20$, $40$, $60$ and $80$ percent of their vertices up to the full graph.
%
The runs are on server 2.
%
The panels show the sizes of both indexes, then the build time of \chainidx and of \cnd run once per size, then the own-level locating and listing time of both indexes.
%
A sample of a fraction $p$ of the vertices keeps about $p^2$ of the edges, so the samples grow in size and in density at once.
%
The largest cliques of \textsf{web-BerkStan} go from $45$ to $202$ vertices.
%
\chainidx grows with the vertices, at $2.9$ to $3.2$ bytes per vertex on \textsf{cit-Patents} and at $5.3$ to $12.6$ bytes per vertex on \textsf{web-BerkStan}, whose cliques grow with the sample.
%
\strees grows with the number of (vertex, size) pairs.
%
The ratio of the two sizes rises along each curve, from $7.7\times$ to $12.1\times$ on \textsf{cit-Patents} and from $6.4\times$ to $19.2\times$ on \textsf{web-BerkStan}.
%
The build time grows faster than the sample: from $0.56$ to $19.5$ seconds as the vertices of \textsf{cit-Patents} grow five times, and from $0.21$ to $65.6$ seconds on \textsf{web-BerkStan}.
%
\cnd once per size grows faster still: its build and peel time divided by the build time of \chainidx rises from $6.6$ to $18$ along the \textsf{cit-Patents} curve and lies between $61$ and $135$ along the \textsf{web-BerkStan} curve.
%
Query latency stays flat: locating stays between $21$ and $28$~ns and listing between $0.09$ and $0.21$~ns per vertex at every sample size.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_scale.pdf}
\caption{Scalability over vertex-induced samples.}\label{fig:scale}
\end{figure*}

\expsection{Against one decomposition per size}
\cnd computes the core values of one size per run, so obtaining every size with it means one run per size.
%
Table~\ref{tab:prior} sums those runs over the sizes $2$ to $s_{\max}$ on \priorgraphs{} (graph, machine) pairs.
%
It reports the end-to-end time of all runs and their build and peel time alone, against the whole build of \chainidx on the same machine.
%
Counting only the build and peel time of \cnd, \chainidx is built faster by \priormin$\times$ on \textsf{com-amazon} (six sizes) to \priormax$\times$ on \webuk{} ($499$ sizes), median \priormedian$\times$.
%
Counting the end-to-end time of \cnd, which reads and sorts the graph for every size, the factors are larger still.
%
The clique tree is built once instead of once per size, and the peel of one size is reused by the next through the certificate of Theorem~\ref{thm:replay} and the bound of Section~\ref{sec:construction}.
%
The ratio grows with the number of sizes: on \textsf{web-BerkStan} ($201$ sizes) the $2.0$ hours of build and peel of \cnd become $66$ seconds, and on \webuk{} $15.7$ hours become $70$ seconds.
%
Table~\ref{tab:prior} also gives the cost of answering a community query without an index: one decomposition at the queried size, seconds to minutes per query on these graphs, against the nanoseconds of Table~\ref{tab:queries}.

\expsection{Case Study I: the best size per query}
We study which clique size best recovers ground-truth communities.
%
Three graphs of the SNAP collection~\cite{leskovec2016snap} come with ground-truth communities, of which SNAP provides the $5{,}000$ of highest quality: \dblp (publication venues), \textsf{com-amazon} (product categories) and \textsf{com-youtube} (user groups).
%
Take a member $v$ of a ground-truth community $D$.
%
For every size $s\le\omg{v}$ and every level $k$, we score the $(s,k)$-core of $v$ by its F1 score against $D$.
%
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the precision and the recall of the core as a guess of $D$.
%
The whole $(s,k)$ space of a query is scanned from the index without listing a community.
%
The size of the intersection is counted by testing, for every member of $D$, whether its own node lies in the subtree of the core.
%
The size of the core comes from its entries.
%
The absolute scale of $k$ differs between sizes, and we compare the best level of each size.
%
The $k$-core at its best level, that is, size $2$, is the first choice.
%
Table~\ref{tab:casegt} compares it with three other choices: the triangle size, $s=3$, at its best level; the best single size for the graph at its best level; and the best size chosen per query, at the own level.
%
The table also gives the best (size, level) chosen per query.
%
Table~\ref{tab:casehist} gives where the best size falls.
%
\sstitle{No single size is right on \dblp.}
The best size spreads over $2$ to $8$.
%
Size $2$ is best for $26$ percent of the queries, size $3$ for $23$ percent, size $4$ for $18$, size $5$ for $13$, and sizes $6$ and above for $20$.
%
Choosing the size and level per query gives an F1 of $0.179$, $3.6\times$ the $0.049$ of the $k$-core and $1.2\times$ the $0.147$ of the best fixed size, $s=5$, at its best level.
%
For $74$ percent of the queries, the remaining ones, some size other than $2$ beats the $k$-core at every level.
%
\sstitle{One size can be enough.}
On \textsf{com-amazon} the triangle size alone reaches $0.824$ against $0.851$ for the per-query choice, $1.7\times$ and $1.8\times$ the $0.474$ of the $k$-core.
%
On \textsf{com-youtube} every size is far from the ground-truth groups, with F1 below $0.04$.
%
Its ground-truth groups are known to be sparse~\cite{dblp}, and the comparison says nothing there.
%
\sstitle{The choice is cheap with the index.}
The per-query scan over every size and level costs $1$ to $50~\mu$s from \chainidx.
%
Without the index, each size of the scan would be one decomposition of the graph.

\expsection{Case Study II: Amazon products across sizes}
We study \textsf{com-amazon} joined with the SNAP product metadata (titles, groups and category paths), available for $334{,}852$ of its $334{,}863$ products.
%
For a query product $q$, the \textit{leaf purity} of a community is the fraction of its members whose leaf category is the leaf category of $q$.
%
Its \textit{subject purity} is the fraction of its members whose subject is the subject of $q$.
%
A subject is the third level of the category tree, such as Jazz, Computers \& Internet or Science Fiction \& Fantasy.
%
Table~\ref{tab:caseamazon} follows $5{,}000$ products, drawn uniformly among those that lie in a triangle, through their own-level community at every size.
%
\sstitle{Purity rises and the communities shrink with the clique size.}
At size $2$ (the $k$-core), three quarters of the $5{,}000$ products sit in one core of $157{,}331$ products at $10$ percent leaf purity.
%
Size $3$ brings the median community to $38$ products at $44$ percent leaf purity.
%
Size $4$ brings it to $11$ products at $70$ percent, and size $5$ to $8$ products at $79$ percent.
%
From size $4$ on, the most common subject of a community covers $99$ percent of its members on average.
%
\sstitle{The communities look like shelves.}
Table~\ref{tab:caseexamples} lists six products.
%
``Kind of Blue'' goes from $36{,}878$ products at size $2$, $1$ percent of them jazz, to $23$ albums of the Blue Note label at size $3$.
%
At size $5$ it is six jazz albums.
%
``Introduction to Algorithms'' goes from the $157{,}331$-product core to $57$ computing books at size $3$ and $13$ theory textbooks at size $4$.
%
The Godfather soundtrack reaches $28$ products at size $5$ at a leaf purity of only $32$ percent.
%
They still form one shelf: the four Godfather soundtracks among albums of Italian-American singers such as Jerry Vale and Lou Monte.
%
The category tree has no name for this community.
%
\sstitle{Practical guideline.}
Size $3$ is the first size at which the median community, $38$ products, is small enough to read as a list.
%
Sizes $4$ and $5$ bring it to a shelf of $8$ to $11$ products at $70$ to $79$ percent leaf purity.
%
Each of these communities is a few ranges, and the six products of Table~\ref{tab:caseexamples} are listed in under $50$~ns at every size above $2$.
